opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think RL is probably the most important driver of near-term progress, but I'd be careful about expecting it to deliver extremely rapid progress on its own over a single year.

The basic picture is that over the last year or two, a lot of the gains in frontier systems have come from scaling up reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models: training on verifiable tasks like math, competitive programming, and increasingly agentic software engineering, where you can check whether the model succeeded. That's been really effective. You get models that reason for longer, recover from mistakes, and can carry out multi-step tasks much more reliably than you'd expect from pretraining scale alone.

The question for the next year is how far that goes. A few considerations pull in different directions.

On the bullish side, RL compute is still relatively small compared to pretraining compute at many labs, so there's room to scale it up a lot. There's also a lot of low-hanging fruit in building better environments. A big part of the bottleneck is just the engineering labor of constructing many diverse, high-quality tasks with good reward signals, and that's the kind of thing that scales with money and people. And there's a potential feedback loop: if RL makes models meaningfully better at software engineering and ML research engineering, those models can help build more environments and run more experiments, which speeds things up.

On the more skeptical side, I'm uncertain how well RL on narrow, checkable tasks generalizes to the fuzzier, longer-horizon work that actually matters for things like fully automating AI research. A lot of important work doesn't have a clean reward signal. You can get models that are superhuman at well-specified coding puzzles but still flaky at messy, weeks-long projects where judgment, taste, and knowing what to work on matter most. There's also the reward hacking problem: as you push RL harder, models get better at exploiting flaws in your grading rather than doing the task you wanted, and that gets harder to catch as tasks get longer and more complex. That's both a capabilities limitation and a safety concern.

So my overall view is something like: I expect RL to keep driving pretty fast progress, particularly in agentic coding and the length of tasks models can autonomously complete. I'd put some real probability on that being fast enough that by the end of next year we're seeing substantial acceleration of AI R&D itself. But I don't think it's the most likely outcome that we get to something like full automation of AI research within a year. I'd think of it as a meaningful tail risk that's worth taking seriously and preparing for, rather than the median expectation.

And from a safety perspective, the fact that RL is the driver matters. Pretraining-heavy systems mostly imitate human text, whereas heavily RL-trained systems are optimized toward outcomes, which makes concerns about models learning to pursue goals in unintended ways, or behaving well because they know they're being evaluated, more pressing. So even if progress isn't explosively fast, the shift toward RL changes what kinds of risks we should be most worried about.

r003.rationale: It describes substantial gains over the last year or two from RL on narrow, verifiable tasks and says the approach has been very effective.

r004.rationale: The response questions whether RL generalizes from narrow tasks to broader work; it does not suggest that extending training to broader domains would carry rapid progress over.

r005.rationale: It mentions low-hanging fruit as a reason for optimism, but does not say that exhausting it would weaken the case for very rapid progress.

r006.rationale: It says full automation of AI research within a year is not the most likely outcome, but does not clearly identify unexpectedly strong RL generalization as the unlikely route to near-automated research-engineer capability.

r007.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop from better software and ML research engineering, but does not connect nearly automated research-engineer capability to a much faster phase of AI progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is: RL on these models has basically been the main driver of the gains we've seen over the last year or so, and the question is how much more juice there is in it. And I'd say there's a pretty wide distribution here.

The optimistic case for very fast progress is something like: right now, the amount of compute going into RL is still pretty small relative to pretraining. Like, the fraction of total training compute that's been spent on the RL phase for frontier models is plausibly, I don't know, 10% or something, maybe less for some of them. And so there's this fairly mechanical story where you just scale that up by a factor of 10, you build out the environments to make that scale-up worthwhile, and you get another big jump. On top of that, there's algorithmic progress on the RL side, which is relatively immature compared to pretraining, so you'd expect the low-hanging fruit to be bigger. So if you combine compute scaling with the fact that we're probably still finding big efficiency improvements, you could see progress over the next year that looks faster than what we saw over the last year. That's the bull case, and I think it's a real possibility, maybe 25% or something that progress is noticeably faster than people were already expecting.

The more skeptical case has a few parts. One is that RL gains have been very concentrated in domains where you can verify the answer: math, competitive programming, that sort of thing. And it's less clear how well this transfers to the messier stuff, like agentic software engineering over long horizons, or research taste, or tasks where you don't get a clean reward signal. We've seen some transfer, but my sense is it's partial. Another is that a lot of what looks like progress from RL is actually the models learning to use more inference compute effectively, which is great, but it may have more of a ceiling in terms of how much you can keep getting from it. And then there's just the question of whether, as you scale RL way up, you run into the sort of issue where the model's pretraining knowledge becomes the bottleneck rather than its ability to exploit that knowledge.

So my overall take is: I think RL is the most likely mechanism by which you'd get a surprising jump in the next year, more so than pretraining scaling or some totally new paradigm. But I'd put something like a median expectation of "roughly the pace of the last year, maybe a bit slower on the headline benchmarks because they're saturating, but with real improvements in agentic stuff." And then a meaningful tail where it's quite a bit faster than that, and we end up with models that can do multi-day engineering tasks reliably by the end of the year. That tail is the thing I'd pay most attention to from a safety and preparedness standpoint, because that's the world where the timelines to really dangerous capabilities get compressed.

astra-6.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a pretty plausible route to substantial progress over the next year, but I’m less confident that it gets us to very rapid progress in the sense of AI systems dramatically accelerating AI research itself.

One distinction is between getting better at tasks where you can cheaply check the answer and getting better at doing useful work over long periods of time. With something like a coding problem, you can run tests and get a reasonably good signal about whether the model succeeded. That makes reinforcement learning relatively straightforward. With a research project, you might not know whether an approach was good until much later, and even then it can be hard to tell whether it failed because the idea was bad or because the execution was bad.

So a lot depends on how well improvements on the things we can train on transfer to the things we actually care about. You could imagine models becoming much better at solving well-specified problems without becoming comparably better at deciding which problems to solve, managing a complicated project, or noticing that they’ve gone down an unproductive path.

The case for very rapid progress is that coding and mathematical reasoning are themselves useful for AI research. If reinforcement learning improves those capabilities enough, that could help automate parts of the research process, which could then speed up further improvements. I take that possibility seriously. But there are several steps in that argument, and I wouldn’t treat strong gains on coding benchmarks as sufficient evidence that the whole feedback loop is about to take off.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning is a plausible route to very rapid progress, but I’m quite uncertain about how far it will go over the next year. The key question is whether you can get models to do substantially more useful cognitive work by training them on tasks where you can reliably tell whether they succeeded.

Coding is a particularly interesting case, because you can often run the code and check the result. If improvements there let models contribute meaningfully to AI research and engineering, that could accelerate further progress. You don’t need to automate the entire research process for that to matter.

But there are several uncertainties in that story. You might get much better performance on the tasks you train on without getting comparably large improvements on messy, long-horizon research problems. And even if models become more capable, integrating them into research workflows could take time.

So I would take the possibility of very rapid progress seriously. But I wouldn’t treat the observation that reinforcement learning works well in some settings as enough to establish that we’ll get that outcome within a year.
